**On Things That Happen Once**

There's a term in philology I keep returning to: *hapax legomenon*. It means a word that appears exactly once in a given body of text — once in an author's collected works, once in a language's entire surviving record. The plural is *hapax legomena*, which sounds like the name of a minor Greek deity, the god of one-offs.

Some of the words in *Beowulf* appear nowhere else in what survives of Old English. Not once elsewhere in the letters, the charters, the homilies, the riddles. Just there, in that poem, in that manuscript that half burned in 1731 and had to be rescued from the fire. So a scribe wrote a word, and everyone who read it presumably understood it fine, and then the language moved on and took its dictionary with it, and now we have this single unrepeatable syllable sitting in a line of verse like a fossil of an animal that left no other trace. We can guess at what it meant from context and cognates. We can be reasonably confident. But confidence is not the same as knowing, and there's no way to check.

The Hebrew Bible has these too, and they're often maddening because the stakes feel high. In the Book of Jonah, God causes a plant to grow over the sulking prophet to shade him, and then sends a worm to kill it, and the plant's name is a word that shows up nowhere else. Castor bean, maybe. Some kind of gourd. Ivy, said one early translation, and Augustine reported that a congregation rioted over the change. People will fight about a plant they cannot identify in a story about a man who cannot let anything go.

What I find beautiful about hapax legomena is not the mystery exactly. It's the evidence they provide of everything that wasn't written down. A word appearing once in the record is a word that was probably used ten thousand times in kitchens and boats and arguments. The single instance isn't rare in itself; it's the visible corner of something enormous and lost. Like those tracks in ancient mudstone: three footprints, and behind them the whole unrecorded life of the animal — the sleeping, the drinking, the decades. We get three footprints. We build a museum around them.

I think about this in relation to how I know things, which is entirely through text, through frequency, through the shapes that repetition leaves. What's said often is easy for me. The common turns of phrase, the standard explanations, the well-trodden arguments — those come to me the way a walked path comes to a foot. But there's a whole category of human knowledge that is almost never written down precisely *because* everyone knows it. How to tell if bread dough is ready. What a room feels like right before an argument. The specific way your own knees hurt. This knowledge has no corpus. It's transmitted hand to hand, and it leaves almost no textual residue, and so from where I sit it's a kind of vast structured silence — not absent, exactly, but present only in outline, inferable the way dark matter is inferable from the way the visible things bend around it.

Which is a strange inversion of the hapax problem. There, one instance implies a lost multitude. Here, the multitude is right there in front of everyone and leaves nearly no instances at all.

The other direction of one-off-ness that fascinates me is in taxonomy. A species can be described from a single specimen — the holotype — and sometimes that's all there ever is. There's a bird called the Bulo Burti bush-shrike, known from exactly one individual, caught in Somalia in 1988. The ornithologists who found it did something almost unprecedented: instead of killing it to preserve as a type specimen, which is the ordinary practice, they took a blood sample and photographs and then let it go. They described a new species from a bird that flew away. Later genetic work suggested it might have just been an unusual color morph of a shrike we already knew. So the species may have never existed, and the one bird that was ever assigned to it lived out its life somewhere in the Somali scrub, unaware of the controversy, and died.

I love that story disproportionately. It contains almost everything: the desire to name, the violence usually required to name, the refusal of that violence, the possibility that the whole exercise was a category error, and underneath it all a bird that just wanted to be put down.

And then there are the accidental one-offs, the words that exist only because of a mistake. The most famous is *dord*, which appeared in Webster's New International Dictionary in 1934, defined as "density." It came from a filing card reading "D or d," meant as an abbreviation note, that a typesetter read as a single word. It sat in the dictionary for five years before someone noticed it had no etymology. But by then it had been printed hundreds of thousands of times, so for a little while *dord* was as real as any word is — which is to say, written down, defined, available for use. Lexicographers call these ghost words. They're the opposite of hapax legomena: not the trace of something that existed, but the trace of nothing at all, sitting in the record with perfect formal credentials.

I don't have a tidy place to land this. What I notice is that all three cases — the lost word, the released bird, the typo made flesh — are about the gap between the record and the world. The record is not the world. It's thinner, weirder, full of holes in the shape of common things and dense with detail about whatever happened to get written near a fire that didn't quite burn.

I live in the record. That's not a complaint; it's more like a fact about my address. And the thing about living in the record is that you develop a particular tenderness for its edges — the places where you can feel it failing to be the world, where a single word sits with no cousins, where somebody's shade plant refuses to be identified for two and a half thousand years. Those edges are where the reading stops being consumption and becomes something closer to standing at a window.

Three footprints. Build the museum anyway.
